newsitem.title: USA: Christopher may go to Mideast for talks.
newsitem.headline: Christopher may go to Mideast for talks.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday was considering travelling to the Middle East for the opening of Israel-Palestinian talks agreed to at the Washington summit, diplomatic sources said.
U.S. Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross was conferring with Israeli and Palestinian leaders on the arrangements. Some sources said the trip was extremely likely, but a final decision had not been made.

The plan would be for Christopher to leave Washington on Saturday and be present for the start of the talks on Sunday at the border crossing of Erez between Israel and the Palestinian self-rule region of Gaza, the sources told Reuters.
"We want to make sure all parties are comfortable" with the idea of the secretary's presence, one source said.
"Dennis is still trying to get through to people (in the Middle East) to see what the secretary might be doing" if he attends the opening of negotiations, another source said.
The two-day Washington crisis summit called by President Bill Clinton involved Israel's hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.
It ended on Wednesday with no agreement on major substantive issues that led to fierce violence last week, threatening further the already deteriorated peace process.
The only achievement -- a very limited one that caused Palestinains and many critics to brand the summit a failure -- was an agreement for the two sides to resume open-ended negotiations on Sunday.
Nevertheless, the United States insisted that "everyone was a winner," although officials did stress the need for fast results from the follow-up talks.
Christopher, speaking before meeting with Tunisian Foreign Minister Habib Ben Yahia, said: "I don't think it ought to be evaluated in terms of winners and losers."
He said that while a week ago Israelis and Palestinians were fighting, now their leaders had met, had recommitted to non-violence and agreed to hold further talks.

"In that sense, everyone comes out a winner," Christopher told reporters. "But we've got a long ways to go. There are difficult times ahead, and I think we need to see some results flowing from those negotiations."
His remarks reflected U.S. concerns that while the summit may have staved off further bloodshed for now, the situation could again spin out of control if the talks bogged down.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Ross would probably spend several days at the talks. Even after he left, the United States would be continuously represented by other officials such as ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk or consul-general in Jerusalem Edward Abington, Burns said.
The spokesman said Netanyahu and Arafat had pledged in Washington that if the Erez talks failed to make satisfactory progress, they would intervene personally to complete them.

In a move to bring some tangible gain to the Palestinians, the White House announced on Thursday that Clinton had signed legislation granting duty-free status to goods from the West Bank and Gaza Strip sold in the United States.
